solution.concept_anchor: Western Ghats faulted escarpment not fold mountain
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because students who associate 'mountain range' with folding mechanics assume the Western Ghats arose similarly to the Himalayas.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a — the Western Ghats are not a fold mountain range; they did not arise from crustal compression.
Eliminate option c — the Western Ghats are younger than the ancient Gondwana breakup sequence but older than Himalayas; they did not form through volcanism in the sense of constructive cones.
Eliminate option d — a horst describes the Satpura Range, formed between two rift valleys; this does not apply to Western Ghats.
Confirm option b — the Western Ghats are a faulted escarpment formed along the western margin of the Deccan Plateau during Gondwanaland rifting and the opening of the Arabian Sea.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students familiar with fold mountains (Himalayas, Aravallis) tend to classify all prominent ranges as fold mountains. The Western Ghats look like a mountain wall from the coastal plain, reinforcing this misconception. However, they are structurally a faulted escarpment — a steep edge of the Deccan Plateau — not a mountain range built by crustal folding. The confusion is compounded because the Western Ghats are indeed ancient (Peninsular block origin, linked to Gondwana breakup) but structurally entirely different from fold mountains.
solution.final_explanation:
The Western Ghats represent one of India's most misunderstood physiographic features. They appear to be a mountain range when viewed from the Kerala or Konkan coast, but geologically they are a faulted escarpment — a steep western edge of the Deccan Plateau that dropped along a fault line during the breakup of Gondwanaland and the consequent opening of the Arabian Sea.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Fold mountains arise from crustal compression (e.g., Himalayas, Aravallis). The Western Ghats formed by faulting, not folding.
• Option (b) — Correct: They are a faulted escarpment of the Peninsular block, formed when the western portion of the Gondwana landmass rifted away and the Arabian Sea was created.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: While the Deccan Traps are volcanic in origin, the Ghats themselves are a structural escarpment, not a volcanic mountain chain.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: A horst is a block uplifted between two grabens — this defines the Satpura Range, not the Western Ghats.

Value Addition:
• The Western Ghats belong to the Peninsular Block — geologically among the most stable regions of India.
• Himalayas are the youngest mountains in India; Aravallis are the oldest fold mountains.
• The Arabian Sea branch of the SW monsoon strikes the escarpment directly, causing intense orographic rainfall.

solution.concept_anchor: Palakkad Gap significance and Western Ghats passes

statement_analysis.statement: Thal Ghat is associated with the Mumbai–Agra National Highway and provides connectivity to the northern Deccan.
statement_analysis.reason: Thal Ghat (also Kasara Ghat) is traversed by NH-3 (now renumbered NH-160), the Mumbai–Agra highway corridor, providing access northward onto the Deccan.

statement_analysis.statement: Palakkad Gap is the narrowest and least significant pass in the Western Ghats in terms of elevation.
statement_analysis.reason: Palakkad Gap (Pal Ghat) is actually the LOWEST and WIDEST break in the Western Ghats, not the narrowest; it is the most significant pass, enabling rail and road connectivity between Kerala and Tamil Nadu and profoundly influencing Kerala's rainfall distribution.

statement_analysis.statement: The highest peak of the Western Ghats, Anamudi, is located in Kerala.
statement_analysis.reason: Anamudi (2,695 m) lies in the Anaimalai Hills within Idukki district, Kerala — it is the highest peak of the Western Ghats and the highest point in India south of the Himalayas.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students who know that 'Palakkad Gap is the most important pass' may incorrectly assume this implies it is also the narrowest, confusing significance with physical size.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Thal Ghat and NH-3 (Mumbai-Agra) connection is standard geography; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Palakkad Gap is the LOWEST and WIDEST, not narrowest; the qualifier 'narrowest' makes this false.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Anamudi (2,695 m) in Kerala is universally accepted as the highest peak of the Western Ghats; Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — this matches option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the trap. Students know the Palakkad Gap is the 'most significant' pass and automatically associate significance with being 'narrow' (like a strategic mountain pass). In reality, the Palakkad Gap is significant precisely because it is the WIDEST and LOWEST break — allowing monsoon winds, railways, and roads to pass through. The word 'narrowest' converts a correct idea into a false statement.
solution.final_explanation:
The Western Ghats are punctuated by a few strategically critical passes that have shaped trade, transport, and climate patterns across peninsular India.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Thal Ghat serves the Mumbai–Agra highway (formerly NH-3), opening the northern Deccan plateau to the west coast.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Palakkad Gap is the LOWEST and WIDEST break in the Western Ghats, not the narrowest. Its low elevation (~300 m) allows moisture-laden monsoon winds to penetrate Kerala from the east and has made it the natural corridor for the Coimbatore–Palakkad railway line.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Anamudi at 2,695 m in the Anaimalai Hills (Idukki, Kerala) is the apex of the Western Ghats and the highest peak in all of peninsular India.

Value Addition:
• Bhor Ghat (NH-4) connects Mumbai to Pune — commercially the most heavily used ghat road.
• Palakkad Gap also creates a rain shadow effect on Tamil Nadu's Coimbatore region.
• Elevation of the Western Ghats increases progressively southward, with the highest elevations concentrated in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

solution.concept_anchor: Western Ghats monsoon asymmetry and rain shadow

statement_analysis.statement: The windward (western) slopes of the Western Ghats receive heavy orographic rainfall primarily from the southwest monsoon.
statement_analysis.reason: The Arabian Sea branch of the SW monsoon strikes the western escarpment, rising orographically and releasing heavy precipitation on the windward side — exceeding 200–400 cm annually in places like Cherrapunji of the Ghats.

statement_analysis.statement: The northeast monsoon contributes significantly to the rainfall received on the windward slopes of the Western Ghats.
statement_analysis.reason: The NE monsoon primarily benefits the eastern coast (Coromandel Coast, Eastern Ghats region). The Western Ghats' windward (western) slopes receive negligible rainfall from the NE monsoon; the NE monsoon winds blow offshore relative to the west coast.

statement_analysis.statement: Cities such as Pune and Nashik experience semi-arid conditions because they lie in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats.
statement_analysis.reason: Located on the leeward (eastern) side of the Western Ghats, Pune and Nashik receive significantly reduced rainfall compared to Mumbai or Mahabaleshwar, making them rain shadow zones despite their proximity to the heavy-rainfall coast.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b would be chosen by students who incorrectly believe Statement 3 is false (since Pune seems too major a city to be 'semi-arid'), making them doubt a correct statement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — SW monsoon and orographic rainfall on windward Western Ghats slopes is well-established; Statement 1 is CORRECT, not the answer.
Evaluate Statement 2 — NE monsoon does NOT contribute significantly to western slopes of Western Ghats; this is factually wrong, so Statement 2 is INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Pune (~700 mm annually) and Nashik are standard examples of rain shadow zones east of Western Ghats; Statement 3 is CORRECT.
Only Statement 2 is incorrect — this matches option d (2 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in Statement 2. Students who know that the NE monsoon is significant for Eastern India may assume it also contributes to the Western Ghats region generally. In reality, the NE monsoon blows from the northeast toward the southwest — it moves offshore when it reaches the west coast, contributing almost nothing to the windward slopes of the Western Ghats. The contrast between how the two monsoon branches affect the two Ghats systems is a recurring UPSC theme.
solution.final_explanation:
The Western Ghats create one of the most dramatic rainfall asymmetries in the world. The SW monsoon's Arabian Sea branch rises abruptly against the escarpment, releasing most of its moisture on the windward (western) side before descending dry on the leeward (eastern) side.

• Statement 1 — Correct: SW monsoon is the primary agent of orographic rainfall on western slopes; this is a fundamental fact.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The NE monsoon blows from the northeast toward the Arabian Sea and is primarily responsible for rainfall on the Coromandel Coast and eastern slopes of the Eastern Ghats. It does not significantly affect the windward slopes of the Western Ghats.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Pune (~700 mm) and Nashik lie in the rain shadow, receiving far less rainfall than windward stations like Mahabaleshwar (~6,000 mm).

Value Addition:
• Major rivers of the Deccan (Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery) originate from the eastern slopes of the Western Ghats, fed by the rain shadow zone's drainage.
• NE monsoon is crucial for Tamil Nadu's agriculture (October–December).
• The rain shadow effect of Western Ghats significantly influences the distribution of cotton cultivation in Maharashtra's Deccan interior.

solution.concept_anchor: Western Ghats WHS six states including Gujarat

statement_analysis.statement: The Western Ghats were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.
statement_analysis.reason: The Western Ghats WHS was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2012, recognising its outstanding universal value as a biodiversity hotspot.

statement_analysis.statement: The Western Ghats WHS encompasses sites across Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Goa, and Maharashtra — five states in total.
statement_analysis.reason: The WHS covers sites across six states, not five — Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra, and Gujarat. The inclusion of Gujarat (Shoolpaneshwar Wildlife Sanctuary area) is frequently missed.

statement_analysis.statement: The Gadgil Committee (2011) recommended more extensive Ecologically Sensitive Area demarcation than the Kasturirangan Committee (2013).
statement_analysis.reason: The Gadgil Committee proposed declaring nearly 64% of the Western Ghats as Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA), while the Kasturirangan Committee recommended a more limited ~37%, making Gadgil's recommendation more extensive and more controversial.

statement_analysis.statement: Silent Valley, Agasthyamalai, and Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve are recognised sites within the Western Ghats biodiversity hotspot.
statement_analysis.reason: All three are core endemic zones within the Western Ghats hotspot, hosting high concentrations of endemic flora and fauna; Silent Valley (Kerala) is especially noted for its undisturbed tropical rainforest.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) tempts students who correctly identify the Gujarat error in Statement 2 but then doubt one of the other three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — UNESCO inscription year 2012 for Western Ghats WHS is standard; correct.
Verify Statement 2 — Five states listed, but the correct number is six; Gujarat is omitted; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3 — Gadgil recommended ~64% ESA vs. Kasturirangan's ~37%; Gadgil was broader; Statement 3 is correct.
Verify Statement 4 — Silent Valley, Agasthyamalai, and Nilgiris are all recognised endemic zones of the Western Ghats hotspot; correct. Three of four statements are correct — option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The standard answer students give is 'five states' — Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Goa, and Maharashtra — because these are the five states most obviously associated with the Western Ghats. Gujarat's inclusion (specifically the Shoolpaneshwar region near the Tapti origin) is consistently missed. This is a classic UPSC entity-swap trap where the omission of one entity converts an otherwise correct-sounding statement into a false one.
solution.final_explanation:
The Western Ghats are one of 36 global biodiversity hotspots and were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012, covering over 900,000 hectares across six states.

• Statement 1 — Correct: UNESCO inscription was confirmed in 2012.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The WHS spans six states — the five commonly cited (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra) plus Gujarat. Omitting Gujarat is the most frequent error in this context.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Gadgil Committee (2011) proposed ~64% of the Ghats as ESA; Kasturirangan (2013) scaled this down to ~37%, attracting less opposition from states with development interests.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Silent Valley, Agasthyamalai, and Nilgiris are flagship endemic zones within the hotspot.

Three statements are correct — option b.

Value Addition:
• Silent Valley National Park (Kerala) famously resisted a hydroelectric dam project in the 1970s–80s.
• The Western Ghats hotspot harbours over 5,000 species of flowering plants, 139 mammal species, and 508 bird species.
• Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF) is the body that designates and monitors global biodiversity hotspots.

solution.concept_anchor: Eastern Ghats hill ranges and their states
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b swaps Nallamala Hills to Odisha and Mahendragiri to Andhra Pradesh, exploiting uncertainty about which ranges fall in which state.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Mahendragiri — it is the highest point in Odisha and is unambiguously in Odisha; this fixes A-3.
Nallamala Hills are the prominent range in Andhra Pradesh (Kurnool-Nellore region); this fixes B-1.
Javadi Hills are clearly in Tamil Nadu (North Arcot/Vellore region); this fixes C-4.

Shevaroy/Servarayan Hills are in Salem district, Tamil Nadu — but if Javadi is Tamil Nadu, Shevaroy must also be TN; verify C-Javadi and D-Shevaroy both TN is consistent; D-2 (Tamil Nadu) completes the match — option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Eastern Ghats are discontinuous and their constituent hill ranges are spread across multiple states with sometimes overlapping or similar-sounding names. Students frequently swap Mahendragiri between Odisha and the southernmost point of Eastern Ghats in Odisha/AP border, or confuse Nallamala (AP) with ranges in Tamil Nadu. The trap is designed so that a student who knows two matches confidently must correctly resolve the remaining two without confusing AP and Odisha ranges.
solution.final_explanation:
The Eastern Ghats are not a single continuous range but a series of disconnected hill systems running in a NE-SW direction across Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu.

Correct matches:
• A (Mahendragiri) — 3 (Odisha): Mahendragiri (1,501 m) is the highest point in the Odisha section of the Eastern Ghats.
• B (Nallamala Hills) — 1 (Andhra Pradesh): Nallamala Hills dominate the interior of AP (Kurnool, Nellore, Prakasam districts), forming the catchment for the Krishna river's lower reaches.
• C (Javadi Hills) — 4 (Tamil Nadu): Javadi Hills lie in Tiruvannamalai and Vellore districts of Tamil Nadu.
• D (Shevaroy/Servarayan Hills) — 2 (Tamil Nadu): Shevaroy Hills (Salem district, TN) are home to the Yercaud hill station.

Trap pairing: Students often place Mahendragiri in AP due to proximity to AP's northern border.

Value Addition:
• The Eastern Ghats receive more rainfall during the NE monsoon (Oct–Dec) than the SW monsoon.
• Charnockite and Khondalite — ancient crystalline rocks — are the dominant geological formations of the Eastern Ghats.
• Jindhagada Peak (~1,690 m, AP) is often cited as the highest peak of the Eastern Ghats overall.

solution.concept_anchor: Anamudi vs Doddabetta — distinct peaks, distinct ranges
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is chosen by students who know both facts are true but do not carefully check whether Doddabetta's being the Nilgiris' highest peak causally explains Anamudi's being South India's highest peak — two unrelated records.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion A correct? — Anamudi (2,695 m) in Anaimalai Hills, Kerala is the highest peak in South India and in all of India south of Himalayas. YES, A is correct.
Step 2: Is Reason R correct? — Doddabetta (2,637 m) is indeed the highest peak of the Nilgiris. YES, R is correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Doddabetta being the highest peak of the Nilgiris does NOT explain why Anamudi is the highest peak of South India. These are two separate peaks in two separate hill ranges (Anaimalai vs. Nilgiris). R is a correct but unrelated fact. Correct option is b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This trap exploits the common confusion between Anamudi and Doddabetta. Many students know that both are high peaks in the southern Western Ghats region and assume they belong to the same range. In reality, Anamudi is in the Anaimalai Hills (Idukki, Kerala) while Doddabetta is in the Nilgiris (Tamil Nadu). The reason describes a real fact about the Nilgiris but has no causal connection to Anamudi's status — making this a classic 'both correct but R does not explain A' assertion-reason.
solution.final_explanation:
The southern Western Ghats host multiple high-altitude peaks across distinct sub-ranges, and distinguishing them is a frequent UPSC challenge.

Assertion (A): Correct — Anamudi at 2,695 m (Anaimalai Hills, Idukki district, Kerala) is the highest peak in peninsular India and all of India south of the Himalayan system.

Reason (R): Correct — Doddabetta at 2,637 m is the highest peak of the Nilgiri Hills and the second highest in South India after Anamudi.

Causal link: R does NOT explain A. These are two independent altitude records for two different ranges. The reason that Doddabetta is Nilgiris' highest has no logical bearing on why Anamudi is South India's highest — Anamudi's position follows from its absolute elevation being greater than all other peninsular peaks, including Doddabetta.

Correct option: b.

Value Addition:
• Anamudi means 'elephant's forehead' in Malayalam.
• Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve was India's first Biosphere Reserve (1986) under UNESCO's Man and Biosphere Programme.
• The Nilgiris are the convergence zone of Western and Eastern Ghats — making them botanically and ecologically unique.

solution.concept_anchor: Geological formation sequence of Indian hill ranges
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c places Deccan Traps before Satpura horst formation, which many students accept since Deccan Traps 'feel' more ancient due to their Gondwana association.
elimination_logic: Aravallis are Pre-Cambrian (~2,500 Ma) — definitively the oldest; they must come first.
Deccan Traps erupted at the K-Pg boundary (~65 Ma, Cretaceous-Eocene transition) — they postdate the Aravallis by over 2,400 million years.

Satpura horst formation is linked to the same Gondwana rift tectonics that produced the Narmada-Tapti grabens — broadly Mesozoic to early Cenozoic, roughly contemporaneous with or slightly after Deccan Traps.
Himalayas formed in the Cenozoic (Eocene-Miocene, ~50–15 Ma) — youngest of all; they come last. Correct sequence: Aravallis → Deccan Traps → Satpura Horst → Himalayas = option b.
solution.final_explanation:
India's major physiographic units formed across vastly different geological time periods, and sequencing them requires understanding the tectonic history of the subcontinent.

Correct sequence:
1. Aravallis (~2,500 Ma, Pre-Cambrian): The oldest fold mountains in India, worn down to stumps by billions of years of erosion.
2. Deccan Traps (~65 Ma, K-Pg boundary): Massive basaltic volcanism associated with the Reunion hotspot, coinciding with the mass extinction event.
3. Satpura Horst (Mesozoic–early Cenozoic): Formed as a horst between the Narmada and Tapti grabens during peninsular rifting.
4. Himalayas (~50 Ma onwards, Cenozoic): The youngest fold mountains, still rising, formed by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates.

Why other options fail: Options a, c, and d misplace either the Aravallis (always oldest) or the Himalayas (always youngest), or incorrectly sequence Deccan Traps relative to the Satpura formation.

Value Addition:
• The Indian Plate began separating from Gondwana ~180 Ma; Himalayan orogeny began ~50 Ma.
• Eastern Ghats (Charnockites) are also Pre-Cambrian, coeval in age with the Aravallis.
• The K-Pg Deccan volcanism debate continues — whether it accelerated or mitigated the asteroid-caused mass extinction is an active research question.

solution.concept_anchor: Satpura horst between Narmada and Tapti grabens
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the Satpura region is between Narmada and Tapti may choose option b (anticline) because anticlines are uplifted structures, confusing fold-based uplift with fault-based uplift.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a hill range uplifted between two river valleys that are themselves structural depressions — this is the hallmark of a horst-graben system, not folding or volcanism.
Eliminate option a (syncline) — a syncline is a downward fold; the uplifted block here is the opposite of a syncline.
Eliminate option b (anticline) — an anticline is an upward fold; uplift here is by faulting, not folding, so 'anticline' is structurally incorrect.
Eliminate option c (graben) — grabens are the sunken blocks (the Narmada and Tapti valleys); the range between them is the uplifted block (horst). Option d (horst) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap here operates through vocabulary confusion: students know the Satpura is 'uplifted' and search for a term meaning 'uplifted structure.' They find 'anticline' — which also describes an uplifted rock structure — and select it. The difference is that anticlines result from compressional folding while a horst results from extensional faulting. The scenario's mention of two adjacent rift valleys (grabens) is the diagnostic clue that identifies the mechanism as block faulting, not folding.
solution.final_explanation:
Tectonic structures can produce elevated landforms through fundamentally different mechanisms, and distinguishing between them is critical for UPSC.

In the scenario, a hill range lies between two parallel river valleys that are themselves structural depressions formed by faulting. This configuration — elevated block flanked by sunken blocks — defines a HORST. The Narmada and Tapti valleys are classic grabens (rift valleys formed by downthrow along faults), and the Satpura Range between them is the classic horst (upthrown block).

• Option (a) — Incorrect: A syncline is a concave fold (downwarped); it cannot produce an elevated range.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: An anticline is a convex fold (upwarped) produced by compression; the mechanism here is extensional faulting, not folding.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Graben describes the sunken valleys (Narmada, Tapti), not the uplifted range between them.
• Option (d) — Correct: Horst precisely describes a block uplifted between two parallel grabens — the Satpura Range is the textbook example in India.

Value Addition:
• Dhupgarh (1,350 m) near Pachmarhi is Satpura's highest peak and the highest point in Madhya Pradesh.
• Pachmarhi is Madhya Pradesh's only hill station, located on the Satpura plateau.
• The Narmada and Tapti are two of India's very few westward-flowing major rivers, flowing through rift valleys rather than normal erosional channels.

solution.concept_anchor: Narmada delta vs estuary and westward-flowing rivers
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the Tapti is also westward-flowing through a rift valley may instinctively pick it as the 'odd one' if they confuse its delta/estuary status with Narmada's.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute — all four rivers listed are peninsular rivers; narrow the shared attribute to drainage pattern and terminus type.
Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi all flow eastward and form large deltas on the Bay of Bengal coast — they share both flow direction and delta formation.
Narmada flows westward and does NOT form a delta — it forms an estuary (ria) near Bharuch (Broach) in the Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay).
Narmada is the odd one out — option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question conflates two attributes simultaneously: eastward vs. westward flow, and delta vs. estuary formation. A student who focuses only on 'westward flow' would correctly identify Narmada as different. But the trap is designed so that students who are less precise might include Tapti (also westward, also an estuary) and become confused. The question presents only Narmada among the four, making the answer unambiguous — Narmada does not form a delta, while the other three (all eastward flowing) do.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests knowledge of river termini and drainage patterns of peninsular rivers.

• Godavari: Flows eastward; forms a large, multi-distributary delta on the Andhra Pradesh coast.
• Krishna: Flows eastward; forms a delta shared with the Godavari delta region.
• Mahanadi: Flows eastward; forms a delta in Odisha, home to the Bhitarkanika mangroves.
• Narmada: Flows WESTWARD through a rift valley (graben); does NOT form a delta. Instead, it forms an estuary (a ria) near Bharuch where it meets the Gulf of Khambhat. Delta formation requires a river to deposit sediment in calm, shallow waters — the Narmada's fast flow through a narrow rift valley prevents significant delta building.

Narmada is the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• Narmada and Tapti are the only two major peninsular rivers flowing westward — both through structural rift valleys.
• Narmada is also unusual in having limited tributaries from the Vindhya (north) side due to the abrupt valley walls.
• The Narmada river valley separates the Vindhyas (north) from the Satpuras (south).

solution.concept_anchor: Deccan Traps black cotton soil and Gondwana coal distinction

statement_analysis.statement: Black cotton soil (Regur) formed primarily through the weathering of Deccan Trap basaltic rocks and is concentrated in the Deccan Plateau region.
statement_analysis.reason: Regur soil forms from the in-situ weathering of basaltic lava of the Deccan Traps; it is rich in calcium, iron, and magnesium, and is concentrated in Maharashtra, parts of MP, Gujarat, and Karnataka.

statement_analysis.statement: The Gondwana rock formations, which are the primary coal-bearing strata in India, are distinct from the Deccan Trap basaltic formations.
statement_analysis.reason: Gondwana rocks (Permian-Carboniferous, ~300–250 Ma) are sedimentary formations containing India's major coal deposits, found in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, MP; they predate and are geologically distinct from the younger Deccan Trap igneous basalts (~65 Ma).

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who conflate Deccan Traps with Gondwana rock formations (both associated with 'Gondwanaland') might reject Statement 2 as incorrect, choosing option c.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Regur/Black cotton soil from weathered Deccan Trap basalt is a standard soil geography fact; correct.
Verify Statement 2 — Gondwana rocks (sedimentary, coal-bearing) are entirely distinct from Deccan Traps (igneous, basaltic); the distinction is geological and temporal; correct.
Both statements are independently correct — option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The confusion between Deccan Traps and Gondwana rocks is a persistent UPSC-relevant misconception. Both are associated with the ancient southern supercontinent (Gondwanaland), leading students to conflate them. However, they are completely different: Gondwana rocks are Permian-age sedimentary formations containing coal, while Deccan Traps are Cretaceous-age volcanic basalt. Statement 2 correctly separates them, and students who conflate the two will incorrectly mark it as false.
solution.final_explanation:
Soil types and rock formations of the Deccan plateau are a frequent source of exam confusion.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Regur (black cotton soil) is the product of in-situ weathering of Deccan Trap basalt. Its black colour derives from titaniferous magnetite and its high clay content makes it self-ploughing. It is ideal for cotton cultivation — hence the name.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Gondwana rocks are sedimentary, Permian-Carboniferous in age, and are India's primary coal repositories (Jharia, Raniganj, Singrauli). Deccan Traps are igneous (basaltic), Cretaceous in age (~65 Ma). They differ in rock type, age, genesis, and geographic distribution.

Both statements are correct — option a.

Value Addition:
• The Deccan Traps eruption near the K-Pg boundary (~66 Ma) is associated with massive environmental disruption possibly contributing to the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs.
• India holds the world's 5th largest coal reserves — predominantly in Gondwana rock formations.
• Laterite soil, another Deccan-associated soil, forms from intense leaching in high-rainfall areas — distinct from Regur.

solution.concept_anchor: Cauvery origin in Western Ghats at Talakaveri
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu) is the strongest distractor because the Cauvery flows through the Nilgiris region and Tamil Nadu students associate it with their state.
elimination_logic: Cauvery's origin point is Talakaveri — a well-established geographic fact placed in Brahmagiri Hills, Coorg district.
Coorg/Kodagu is in Karnataka, on the western slopes of the Western Ghats — not in Tamil Nadu.
Eliminate all options that place the origin in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, or the Eastern Ghats.
Option b (Western Ghats, Kodagu district, Karnataka) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Cauvery river dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu has made students associate the Cauvery strongly with Tamil Nadu. However, the river originates in Karnataka's Kodagu (Coorg) district at Talakaveri, on the western slopes of the Western Ghats. Students who conflate the river's political controversy with its geographic origin often incorrectly place the source in Tamil Nadu or the Nilgiris.
solution.final_explanation:
The Cauvery (Kaveri) is one of the most significant rivers of peninsular India, flowing eastward from the Western Ghats across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu to the Bay of Bengal.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Brahmagiri Hills are correct (Talakaveri is in Brahmagiri), but Wayanad is in Kerala, not where the source lies. Wayanad borders Coorg but the source is in Coorg/Kodagu, Karnataka.
• Option (b) — Correct: Talakaveri is located in the Brahmagiri Hills, Kodagu (Coorg) district, Karnataka, on the eastern slopes of the Western Ghats.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Nilgiris are in Tamil Nadu and are associated with the Cauvery's middle course, not its source.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Eastern Ghats do not source the Cauvery; the river cuts through them on its way to the sea.

Value Addition:
• Cauvery supports the Krishnarajasagara (KRS) dam — a major irrigation source for Karnataka.
• The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal awarded the final order in 2007.
• Tungabhadra, a major tributary of Krishna, also originates from the Western Ghats.

solution.concept_anchor: Guru Shikhar highest peak of Aravallis in Mt Abu
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the Aravallis are the oldest mountains in India may pair them with 'Cambrian age' instead of Pre-Cambrian, a temporal-swap trap.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a — Aravallis extend from Delhi to Palanpur (Gujarat), not from Delhi to Jodhpur; Jodhpur is west of the Aravallis, not their terminus.
Eliminate option b — Aravallis are Pre-Cambrian (~2,500 Ma), not Cambrian; Cambrian is ~540 Ma.
Eliminate option d — Guru Shikhar is at Mt. Abu in Rajasthan, not in Haryana; this is a geographic swap.
Option c is correct — Aravallis act as a climatic divide in Rajasthan, with the Thar Desert to the west and relatively better-watered eastern Rajasthan receiving some monsoon rainfall.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Two strong distractors operate here: Option b exploits the 'oldest' label — students know Aravallis are old and may accept 'Cambrian' without recalling the precise Pre-Cambrian designation. Option d correctly names Guru Shikhar but wrongly places it in Haryana instead of Rajasthan's Mt. Abu, testing geographic precision. Only option c correctly states the Aravallis' well-established role as a climatic divide separating the Thar Desert from eastern Rajasthan.
solution.final_explanation:
The Aravalli Range is one of India's most geologically and geographically significant features.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Aravallis run from Raisina Hill (Delhi) in the northeast to Palanpur in Gujarat in the southwest, approximately 800 km. Jodhpur is not the terminus — it lies to the west of the range.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Aravallis are Pre-Cambrian in age (~2,500 Ma), not Cambrian (~540 Ma). Pre-Cambrian and Cambrian are distinct geological eras separated by nearly 2,000 million years.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Aravallis act as a climatic divide — the arid Thar Desert lies to the northwest while the eastern Rajasthan plains receive some SW monsoon rainfall due to the partial protection of the range.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Guru Shikhar (1,722 m), the highest peak of the Aravallis, is located at Mt. Abu in the Sirohi district of Rajasthan, not in Haryana.

Value Addition:
• The Aravallis are heavily eroded — many sections are mere ridges and hillocks today.
• Gaps in the Aravallis allow cold, dust-laden northwestern winds to reach Delhi and Gangetic plains.
• Aravalli afforestation is part of India's efforts to check the eastward spread of the Thar Desert.

solution.concept_anchor: Eastern Ghats NE monsoon vs Western Ghats SW monsoon

statement_analysis.statement: The Bay of Bengal branch of the southwest monsoon is effectively blocked by the Eastern Ghats and does not penetrate the interior of the Deccan Plateau.
statement_analysis.reason: The Eastern Ghats are a discontinuous, low-elevation range and do NOT effectively block the Bay of Bengal branch of the SW monsoon; the monsoon readily penetrates the interior through gaps and river valleys, reaching the Deccan Plateau and even the rain shadow zone of Western Ghats.

statement_analysis.statement: The Satpura and Vindhya ranges act as secondary orographic barriers influencing rainfall distribution across central India.
statement_analysis.reason: Though not as dramatic as the Western Ghats, the Satpuras and Vindhyas do deflect and influence the central India monsoon rainfall distribution, particularly for the SW monsoon's Arabian Sea branch moving northward.

statement_analysis.statement: The Eastern Ghats receive more rainfall during the northeast monsoon (October–December) than during the southwest monsoon season.
statement_analysis.reason: The Eastern Ghats and the Coromandel Coast face the Bay of Bengal and lie directly in the path of the NE monsoon (retreating monsoon), which originates over the Bay of Bengal and deposits significant rainfall on the eastern slopes during October–December — more than they receive from the SW monsoon.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Statements 2 and 3 are likely correct may pause on Statement 1 and, recalling that 'Eastern Ghats are lower,' incorrectly assume they do block the monsoon to some significant extent, choosing option b (2 and 3 only is the correct choice but students might reconsider Statement 3).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Eastern Ghats are discontinuous and low; the Bay of Bengal branch of SW monsoon does penetrate the interior; Statement 1 is false.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Satpuras and Vindhyas as secondary orographic influences on central India monsoon is well-established; Statement 2 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 3 — Eastern Ghats / Coromandel Coast receive peak rainfall during NE monsoon (Oct-Dec), not SW monsoon; this is a well-known contrast with the Western Ghats pattern; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 contains a scope-extension trap: students know the Eastern Ghats are 'less effective' barriers and may read 'does not penetrate' as extreme but plausible, especially if they confuse 'reduced rainfall' with 'blocked.' The reality is that the Bay of Bengal branch actively crosses the Eastern Ghats, reaching far into the Deccan interior — the Eastern Ghats are too discontinuous and low to block it.
solution.final_explanation:
The differential impact of the two monsoon branches on India's major hill ranges is a core examination theme.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Eastern Ghats are broken by rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna) and average only ~600 m in height. The Bay of Bengal branch of the SW monsoon passes through these gaps and penetrates the interior, rendering Statement 1 false.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Satpura and Vindhya ranges function as secondary orographic influences, shaping rainfall distribution across Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra's interior.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The eastern coastal plains and Eastern Ghats receive their peak annual rainfall from the NE (retreating) monsoon. Coastal AP, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha record significant October–December rainfall, contrasting sharply with the Western Ghats' July–September peak.

Value Addition:
• Chennai receives about 60% of its annual rainfall from the NE monsoon — one of the highest NE monsoon dependencies of any major Indian city.
• The SW monsoon contributes >80% of rainfall on the Western Ghats' windward side.
• The Coromandel Coast (Tamil Nadu/southern AP) is one of the few regions in India where NE monsoon > SW monsoon in annual rainfall contribution.

solution.concept_anchor: Meghalaya Hills Peninsular origin not Himalayan

statement_analysis.statement: The Shillong Plateau is a detached portion of the Peninsular Plateau, separated from the main peninsular block by the Brahmaputra valley (Assam gap).
statement_analysis.reason: The Shillong Plateau is geologically a part of the ancient Peninsular block, composed of Precambrian crystalline rocks, physically separated from the main Deccan/Peninsular plateau by the alluvial Brahmaputra (Assam) valley — not part of the Himalayan system.

statement_analysis.statement: The extraordinary rainfall at Mawsynram and Cherrapunji is primarily caused by their location at high altitude on the Khasi Hills, which directly intercept Bay of Bengal moisture through a funnel-shaped topography.
statement_analysis.reason: The Khasi Hills' south-facing, funnel-shaped valleys channel and concentrate Bay of Bengal moisture-laden winds upward, producing some of the world's highest rainfall at Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (Sohra).

statement_analysis.statement: The Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia Hills are part of the Himalayan foothills system, geologically connected to the eastern Himalayan ranges.
statement_analysis.reason: The Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia Hills are sub-ranges of the Meghalaya Plateau, which is geologically Peninsular (ancient crystalline Pre-Cambrian rocks), NOT part of the Himalayan fold mountain system — despite their northeastern location.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Statement 1 is correct (Shillong Plateau is Peninsular) may incorrectly accept Statement 3 as also correct, assuming 'northeastern location implies Himalayan connection.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Shillong Plateau as a detached Peninsular block is a standard geography fact; Statement 1 is CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Funnel-shaped topography of Khasi Hills concentrating Bay of Bengal moisture is the accepted explanation for Cherrapunji/Mawsynram rainfall; Statement 2 is CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Garo, Khasi, Jaintia Hills are Peninsular in geological origin, NOT Himalayan; Statement 3 is INCORRECT.
Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — option b (3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Meghalaya Hills' northeastern location creates a powerful geographic intuition that they must be Himalayan. Students unfamiliar with geological classification of the Shillong Plateau may automatically categorize the Garo-Khasi-Jaintia system as an eastern extension of the Himalayan foothills. The key test is rock type: the Meghalaya Plateau is composed of ancient Pre-Cambrian crystalline rocks (granite, gneiss) identical to the Peninsular block, entirely unlike the folded sedimentary formations of the Himalayan system.
solution.final_explanation:
The Meghalaya Plateau represents one of India's most important yet often misunderstood physiographic units.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Shillong Plateau is physically separated from the main Peninsular block by the broad alluvial Brahmaputra valley but shares its geological character (ancient crystalline rocks).
• Statement 2 — Correct: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji owe their extraordinary rainfall to the funnel geometry of south-facing Khasi Hills, which lift and concentrate the moisture-laden Bay of Bengal winds — producing annual rainfall exceeding 11,000 mm.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia Hills are sub-divisions of the Meghalaya Plateau, which is a Peninsular (Precambrian crystalline) formation. They have no geological connection to the Himalayan fold mountain system.

Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — option b.

Value Addition:
• Mawsynram receives slightly more annual rainfall than Cherrapunji on average; both compete for the world's wettest place title.
• The Brahmaputra flows through a narrow gorge between the Himalayas and the Shillong Plateau — one of the world's most dramatic river gorges.
• Sixth Schedule of the Constitution applies to tribal autonomous councils in Meghalaya (Garo, Khasi, Jaintia Hill districts).

solution.concept_anchor: Shola forests restricted to high-altitude Western Ghats only

statement_analysis.statement: Shola forests are a montane grassland-forest mosaic found exclusively at elevations above 1,500 m in the Western Ghats.
statement_analysis.reason: Shola forests are unique high-altitude (>1,500 m) ecosystems of the Western Ghats — characterised by patches of stunted evergreen forest in hollows surrounded by montane grasslands — found in Nilgiris, Anaimalai, and Palani ranges; they are NOT found in the Eastern Ghats.

statement_analysis.statement: Tropical wet evergreen forests in the Western Ghats are found on both windward (western) and leeward (eastern) slopes equally.
statement_analysis.reason: Tropical wet evergreen forests are concentrated on the windward (western/high-rainfall) slopes; leeward (eastern) slopes transition to semi-evergreen and moist deciduous forests due to reduced rainfall in the rain shadow zone.

statement_analysis.statement: Teak and sal are the dominant species in the tropical dry deciduous forests of the Eastern Ghats and Deccan interior.
statement_analysis.reason: Tropical dry deciduous forests — dominant in the Eastern Ghats and Deccan interior — are characterised by teak (Tectona grandis) and sal (Shorea robusta) as commercially important species, along with tendu, mahua, and bamboo.

statement_analysis.statement: The Satpura-Vindhya region supports major tiger habitats, including Satpura, Kanha, and Pench Tiger Reserves.
statement_analysis.reason: The central Indian tiger landscape, anchored in the Satpura-Vindhya hill system, contains some of India's most significant tiger reserves — Satpura (MP), Kanha (MP), and Pench (MP/Maharashtra) — all within the tropical moist to dry deciduous forest zone.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Only two) is chosen by students who correctly identify Statement 2 as wrong but also incorrectly doubt Statement 3, assuming 'sal is only northern/Himalayan foothills.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Shola forests exclusive to high-altitude Western Ghats is a well-established ecological fact; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — Wet evergreen forests dominate windward slopes; leeward slopes have semi-evergreen/moist deciduous; 'equally' makes this false.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Teak and sal dominate tropical dry deciduous forests of Eastern Ghats and Deccan interior; correct.
Evaluate Statement 4 — Satpura, Kanha, Pench are flagship central Indian tiger reserves in the Satpura-Vindhya landscape; correct. Three of four are correct — option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap is in Statement 2 — the word 'equally' converts a partially true statement into a false one. Wet evergreen forests do occur on eastern slopes too in some transition zones, but the emphasis on 'equally' is the distortion. Additionally, some students believe sal is only a northern/Himalayan foothill species (associated with Terai), incorrectly marking Statement 3 as false when it is actually found across central and eastern India in dry deciduous forests.
solution.final_explanation:
Forest type distribution across India's hill ranges reflects underlying climate, elevation, and soil patterns.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Shola forests exist only above 1,500 m in the Western Ghats — not in the Eastern Ghats, making them a uniquely Western Ghats-associated ecosystem.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Wet evergreen forests are confined to the windward (western) slopes with heavy rainfall. Leeward slopes transition to semi-evergreen and moist deciduous forests as rainfall decreases.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Teak and sal are the twin dominant species of central Indian and Eastern Ghats dry deciduous forests — critical for India's timber economy and wildlife habitats.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Satpura, Kanha, and Pench (all in Madhya Pradesh) form the core of the central Indian tiger corridor in the Satpura-Vindhya landscape.

Three statements are correct — option a.

Value Addition:
• Shola grassland-forest mosaics are critically important watersheds for rivers originating in the Nilgiris-Anaimalai system.
• India has 53 Tiger Reserves (as of 2023); the central Indian landscape holds the maximum concentration.
• Sal forests are also found in the Shivalik foothills and northeastern India, but dominate central India's deciduous belt.

solution.concept_anchor: Fifth Schedule vs Sixth Schedule tribal areas
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who have encountered the term 'Scheduled Areas' in the context of northeastern tribes may instinctively associate all hill tribal areas with the Sixth Schedule.
elimination_logic: Recall that the Fifth Schedule provides for administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
The Sixth Schedule applies specifically to tribal areas in the northeastern states (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram).
The Satpura-Vindhya, Eastern Ghats, and Western Ghats tribal regions are in mainland India (MP, Odisha, AP, Maharashtra, Kerala) — these fall under the Fifth Schedule.
Option c correctly identifies the Fifth Schedule as applicable to these mainland hill tribal regions.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Fifth Schedule–Sixth Schedule distinction is a classic UPSC conflation trap. Both schedules deal with tribal areas and tribal self-governance, making them easy to confuse. The critical differentiator is geography: the Sixth Schedule applies only to tribal areas in four northeastern states (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram), creating Autonomous District Councils. The Fifth Schedule covers all other Scheduled Areas across mainland India, including hill ranges like the Satpuras, Eastern Ghats, and Western Ghats. A student who knows one of the schedules but confuses their regional scope will answer incorrectly.
solution.final_explanation:
India's constitutional framework for tribal administration is divided geographically between two distinct schedules.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Seventh Schedule deals with the division of legislative powers between Union and States, not tribal areas.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Sixth Schedule creates Autonomous District Councils for tribal administration in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram only — the four northeastern states.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Fifth Schedule applies to Scheduled Areas in all other tribal regions — including the Satpura-Vindhya belt (Gond, Bhil tribes), Eastern Ghats (Kondh, Chenchu, Savara), and Western Ghats (Warli, Soliga, Toda).
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Ninth Schedule protects certain laws from judicial review — it has no relevance to tribal administration.

Value Addition:
• The Niyamgiri Hills (Odisha) bauxite mining case — involving the Dongria Kondh tribe — is a landmark in tribal rights and Fifth Schedule application.

solution.concept_anchor: Western vs Eastern Ghats structural and hydrological differences

statement_analysis.statement: The Western Ghats run in a roughly north-south (N-S) direction and form a clear watershed between rivers draining to the Arabian Sea and those draining to the Bay of Bengal.
statement_analysis.reason: The Western Ghats trend roughly N-S along the west coast and act as the primary watershed of peninsular India — rivers to their west flow into the Arabian Sea while those to their east (Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery) flow to the Bay of Bengal.

statement_analysis.statement: The Eastern Ghats run in a NE-SW direction and form a well-defined watershed that prevents rivers from the interior from reaching the Bay of Bengal directly.
statement_analysis.reason: The Eastern Ghats run in a NE-SW direction (correct), but they do NOT form a well-defined watershed — in fact, major peninsular rivers (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery) cut THROUGH the Eastern Ghats on their way to the Bay of Bengal rather than being blocked by them.

statement_analysis.statement: The average elevation of the Western Ghats (900–1,200 m) is significantly higher than that of the Eastern Ghats (~600 m average).
statement_analysis.reason: Western Ghats average 900–1,200 m with a maximum of 2,695 m (Anamudi), while the Eastern Ghats average approximately 600 m with a maximum of ~1,690 m (Jindhagada/Arma Konda region) — a significant difference in elevation.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know the Eastern Ghats run NE-SW may accept Statement 2 entirely (including the false watershed claim) because the directional fact is correct, missing the partial-truth trap.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — N-S trend and watershed role of Western Ghats are correct; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2 — NE-SW direction of Eastern Ghats is correct BUT the 'well-defined watershed' claim is false; rivers cut THROUGH the Eastern Ghats; partial-truth trap makes Statement 2 incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Elevation comparison (WG 900-1200 m avg vs EG ~600 m avg) is accurate; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap: the NE-SW direction of the Eastern Ghats is correct, making the first half of the statement accurate and building student confidence. But the claim that they form a 'well-defined watershed preventing rivers from reaching the Bay of Bengal' is the exact opposite of what happens — the Eastern Ghats are cut through by major rivers, making them porous to drainage rather than a barrier. Students who read quickly and validate the direction fact will accept the entire statement.
solution.final_explanation:
Comparing the two Ghats systems reveals fundamental structural and hydrological differences.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Western Ghats' N-S orientation and continuous nature make them an effective watershed separating Arabian Sea drainage (short, west-flowing rivers like Periyar, Sharavathi) from Bay of Bengal drainage (long, east-flowing rivers like Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: While the NE-SW directional trend is accurate, the Eastern Ghats are NOT a watershed. The Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Cauvery all breach the Eastern Ghats through gorges, flowing directly into the Bay of Bengal.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Western Ghats are consistently higher (average 900–1,200 m, max 2,695 m) compared to Eastern Ghats (average ~600 m, max ~1,690 m).

Value Addition:
• The Western Ghats are continuous while the Eastern Ghats are discontinuous — this is the most fundamental structural difference.
• The Western Ghats receive rainfall from the SW monsoon (windward); Eastern Ghats from the NE monsoon.
• East-flowing rivers from the Western Ghats form deltas; west-flowing rivers are shorter, faster, and power-rich.

solution.concept_anchor: Vindhyas plateau edge escarpment not strict watershed
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts (Vindhyas as historical divide and their east-west orientation) may assume R's geological character explains A's historical significance without examining the causal logic carefully.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion A correct? — The Vindhya Range has historically functioned as a cultural and geographical divide between Aryavarta (north) and Dakshinapatha (south). YES, A is correct.

Step 2: Is Reason R correct? — The Vindhyas are more accurately described as a plateau edge/escarpment running east-west than as a true mountain range formed by folding or faulting. YES, R is correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — The historical significance of the Vindhyas as a divide between north and south India is a cultural-political-ecological reality that existed because of the physical barrier the range (even as an escarpment) posed, not BECAUSE it is structurally an escarpment rather than a fold mountain. R describes the structural nature but does not causally explain WHY it became a historical divide. Correct option is b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a subtle causal trap. Both A (historical divide) and R (escarpment, not fold mountain) are factually true. A student focused on verifying individual facts will confirm both and instinctively choose option a. The trap is that R's structural description does not provide the causal mechanism for A's historical significance — the Vindhyas became a divide because they posed a physical barrier to movement and climate, not specifically because they are structurally an escarpment rather than a fold mountain.
solution.final_explanation:
The Vindhya Range has defined the cultural and political geography of the Indian subcontinent for millennia.

Assertion (A): Correct — Classical texts consistently identify the Vindhyas as the boundary between Aryavarta (the northern Indo-Gangetic civilization) and Dakshinapatha (the southern route/Deccan), making it one of India's oldest geographic divides.

Reason (R): Correct — The Vindhyas are not a folded or faulted mountain range in the strict tectonic sense; they are the northern eroded escarpment edge of the Deccan Plateau, running east-west from Gujarat through Madhya Pradesh to Mirzapur (UP).

Causal link: R does not explain A. The historical significance of the Vindhyas as a north-south divide stems from their role as a physical barrier to movement, climate transition, and cultural exchange — not from the specific structural character (escarpment vs. fold mountain) described in R.

Correct option: b.

Value Addition:
• The Son River originates from the Amarkantak plateau (where Vindhyas and Satpuras meet) and flows northward into the Ganga.
• Chambal and Betwa rivers originate north of the Vindhyas and drain into the Yamuna/Ganga — not into the Deccan drainage.
• Amarkantak in MP is the source of three rivers: Son (north), Narmada (west), and Johila.

solution.concept_anchor: West-flowing rivers of Western Ghats origin
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Sharavathi is a well-known hydropower river (Jog Falls) may forget it flows westward and doubt its inclusion, instead suspecting Periyar.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute — all should be short, high-gradient, west-flowing rivers originating from the Western Ghats.
Periyar — flows westward from Western Ghats into Kerala; belongs to the group.
Sharavathi — flows westward from Western Ghats in Karnataka, forms Jog Falls; belongs to the group.
Bharathapuzha — flows westward from Anamalai/Palakkad region through Kerala into Arabian Sea; belongs to the group.
Tungabhadra — a major tributary of Krishna, flows EASTWARD to the Bay of Bengal; it does NOT belong to the west-flowing Western Ghats rivers group — option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Tungabhadra originates in the Western Ghats (Varaha Parvata) but flows eastward to join the Krishna, eventually reaching the Bay of Bengal. Students who recall that Tungabhadra comes from the Western Ghats may place it in the same group as Periyar and Sharavathi, ignoring the flow direction. The entity-swap trap here substitutes an eastern-flowing river for western-flowing ones, relying on students focusing on origin rather than drainage direction.
solution.final_explanation:
The Western Ghats are the source of both east-flowing and west-flowing rivers, and distinguishing between them is important.

• Periyar: Originates in the Western Ghats (Cardamom Hills), flows westward through Kerala into the Arabian Sea — belongs to the group.
• Sharavathi: Originates in the Western Ghats (Shimoga, Karnataka), flows westward, famous for creating Jog Falls (Gerusoppe Falls) — belongs to the group.
• Bharathapuzha: Second longest river in Kerala, originates in the Anaimalai/Palakkad region, flows westward through Palakkad Gap into the Arabian Sea — belongs to the group.
• Tungabhadra: Originates in the Western Ghats, but flows EASTWARD as a major tributary of the Krishna, eventually reaching the Bay of Bengal — does NOT belong.

Tungabhadra is the odd one out — option c.

Value Addition:
• Jog Falls (Sharavathi) is India's highest plunge waterfall (~253 m).
• Periyar is Kerala's longest river and supports the Idukki hydroelectric project.
• West-flowing rivers of Western Ghats have high hydropower potential due to steep gradients despite their short length.

solution.concept_anchor: Aravallis oldest fold mountains Western Ghats Peninsular escarpment

statement_analysis.statement: The Aravallis are the oldest fold mountains in India, with a geological age of approximately 2,500 million years (Pre-Cambrian).
statement_analysis.reason: The Aravallis are universally recognised as the oldest fold mountain range in India (~2,500 Ma, Pre-Cambrian), making them among the oldest mountain ranges in the world; they are highly eroded today.

statement_analysis.statement: The Western Ghats, being older than the Himalayas, belong to the same fold mountain category as the Aravallis.
statement_analysis.reason: While the Western Ghats are indeed older than the Himalayas (belonging to the ancient Peninsular block), they are NOT fold mountains — they are a faulted escarpment formed by rifting along the western margin of the Deccan Plateau during Gondwanaland breakup, structurally completely different from fold mountains like the Aravallis or Himalayas.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know 'Western Ghats are older than Himalayas' may assume the second part (fold mountain category) is also correct without separately evaluating the structural type.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Aravallis as Pre-Cambrian (~2,500 Ma) oldest fold mountains is a standard fact; correct.

Verify Statement 2 — Western Ghats are older than Himalayas (true), BUT they are NOT fold mountains — they are a faulted escarpment; the statement conflates age (true) with structural type (false), making Statement 2 incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The UPSC trap embedded in Statement 2 is the temporal-swap variant: the first clause ('Western Ghats are older than Himalayas') is true and builds confidence. The second clause ('belong to the same fold mountain category as Aravallis') is the false element. The trap exploits the fact that UPSC explicitly notes 'Western Ghats are older than Himalayas but formed differently' — students who memorise the age comparison without internalising the structural difference will mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Age and structural origin are two independent attributes of mountain ranges, and confusing them is a common UPSC pitfall.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Aravallis formed approximately 2,500 Ma ago through crustal folding during the Precambrian, making them the oldest fold mountains in India. Erosion over billions of years has reduced them to low, broken ridges.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Western Ghats are indeed older than the Himalayas (Peninsular block vs. Cenozoic origin), but this does not make them fold mountains. The Western Ghats formed as a faulted escarpment through rifting and block faulting along the western Deccan margin — not through crustal compression and folding. Structurally, they are entirely different from the Aravallis.

Value Addition:
• Peninsular India's geological stability contrasts sharply with the seismically active Himalayan zone.
• Both Aravallis and the Peninsular plateau are composed of ancient crystalline and metamorphic rocks (granite, gneiss, charnockite).
• The term 'escarpment' refers to a steep slope at the edge of a plateau — applicable to both the Western Ghats and portions of the Vindhyan edge.

solution.concept_anchor: Nilgiris first Biosphere Reserve India 1986
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve (established 1988) was India's first UNESCO MAB-recognized reserve may confuse 'first in India' with 'first internationally recognized.'
elimination_logic: Recall that India's first Biosphere Reserve was established in 1986 under the UNESCO Man and Biosphere Programme.
Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve (Tamil Nadu-Kerala-Karnataka tri-junction) was designated first — 1986.
Nanda Devi (1988), Gulf of Mannar (1989), and Sundarbans (1989) all came after Nilgiris.
The correct completion is Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve — option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The confusion between 'first Biosphere Reserve of India' and 'first UNESCO-recognized Biosphere Reserve of India' is a classic UPSC entity-swap trap. Nilgiris (1986) was India's first designated Biosphere Reserve nationally. Nanda Devi was among the first to receive international UNESCO recognition under MAB (in 1988). Students who conflate the two dates and programs choose Nanda Devi for 'first' — which is incorrect for the national designation.
solution.final_explanation:
India's Biosphere Reserve programme is managed under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in coordination with UNESCO's Man and Biosphere (MAB) Programme.

• Option (a) — Correct: Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve was established in 1986, making it India's first Biosphere Reserve. It spans the tri-state region of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka, covering the Nilgiris, Anaimalai, and Wayanad hills.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve (Uttarakhand) was established in 1988 — second or third in the national sequence, not first.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve was designated in 1989 — a marine biosphere reserve, not the first.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve (West Bengal) was also designated in 1989.

Value Addition:
• India currently has 18 Biosphere Reserves recognized by UNESCO under MAB (as of 2023).
• Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve is home to the Toda, Kota, Kurumba, and Irula tribal communities.
• The Nilgiris is also India's first Elephant Reserve.

solution.concept_anchor: Bhor Ghat Mumbai-Pune NH-4 connectivity
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who confuse Thal Ghat and Bhor Ghat (both on the Mumbai approaches) often assign NH-4 to Thal Ghat and NH-3 to Bhor Ghat — the exact reversal of the correct answer.
elimination_logic: Recall: Thal Ghat is associated with the Mumbai-Agra highway (NH-3, now NH-160) — northward connectivity.
Bhor Ghat is the pass on the Mumbai-Pune route — historically NH-4 (now NH-48), providing southeastern connectivity toward Pune and beyond.
Eliminate option a — it assigns NH-3 to Bhor Ghat, which is Thal Ghat's route.

Eliminate options c and d — option c places Palakkad Gap in Karnataka (it is on Kerala-Tamil Nadu border); option d incorrectly describes Palakkad Gap as narrowest (it is the widest and lowest). Option b is correct: Bhor Ghat is on the Mumbai-Pune route.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Thal Ghat and Bhor Ghat are both on highways leading out of Mumbai, making them highly confusable. Thal Ghat (Kasara) goes northeast toward Nashik/Agra; Bhor Ghat (Khandala/Lonavala) goes east-southeast toward Pune. Students who know both names but have not anchored them to specific highways or destinations will reverse the pairing. Option a is crafted to exploit exactly this reversal.
solution.final_explanation:
India's Western Ghats passes are critical transport corridors connecting the Konkan coast to the Deccan Plateau.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Bhor Ghat is NOT on the Mumbai-Agra route. That is Thal Ghat (NH-3/NH-160). This option reverses the two ghat assignments.
• Option (b) — Correct: Bhor Ghat (Khandala-Lonavala area) carries the Mumbai-Pune corridor, historically NH-4 (now NH-48). It is one of the most commercially critical passes in India.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Palakkad Gap (Pal Ghat) is on the Kerala-Tamil Nadu border, not in Karnataka. It connects Palakkad (Kerala) with Coimbatore (Tamil Nadu).
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Palakkad Gap is the LOWEST and WIDEST break in the Western Ghats — not the narrowest. Its low elevation (~300 m) is precisely what makes it significant.

Value Addition:
• Bhor Ghat was originally engineered for the Great Indian Peninsula Railway in the 1860s — one of India's great Victorian engineering achievements.
• The Expressway (Mumbai-Pune) and the older NH-48 both traverse the Bhor Ghat section.
• Palakkad Gap allows both the Coimbatore-Palakkad railway and significant monsoon moisture to pass through.

solution.concept_anchor: Deccan Traps basalt stepped escarpment Maharashtra K-Pg boundary

statement_analysis.statement: The stepped, layered appearance of the Western Ghats escarpment in Maharashtra is largely a result of the horizontal basaltic lava flows of the Deccan Traps.
statement_analysis.reason: The Deccan Trap basalt flows, laid down in successive horizontal layers, create the characteristic stepped ('trap' derives from Swedish 'trappa' meaning stair) appearance of the escarpment, especially visible in the Sahyadris of Maharashtra.

statement_analysis.statement: The Deccan Traps eruption occurred at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary (~65 Ma) and is associated with significant environmental disruption.
statement_analysis.reason: Deccan Traps volcanism (~66 Ma) occurred near the K-Pg (Cretaceous-Paleogene) boundary, producing massive volcanic gases that may have contributed to or compounded the end-Cretaceous mass extinction event alongside the Chicxulub asteroid impact.

statement_analysis.statement: The Gondwana rock formations and the Deccan Trap basalts together form a continuous geological sequence in the Deccan Plateau.
statement_analysis.reason: Gondwana rocks (Permian-Carboniferous, ~300–250 Ma) are older sedimentary formations separated from the Deccan Trap basalts (~66 Ma) by nearly 200 million years; they are geologically distinct and not a continuous sequence — Gondwana rocks are coal-bearing sedimentary strata while Deccan Traps are volcanic igneous basalt.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who conflate Gondwana and Deccan Trap as both being 'ancient geological formations of the Deccan region' may accept Statement 3 as plausible and choose option d (all three correct).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Stepped appearance of Maharashtra's escarpment from horizontal basalt flows is a fundamental Deccan Trap geography fact; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — K-Pg boundary (~65-66 Ma) association with Deccan Traps and mass extinction is well-established; correct.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Gondwana rocks (sedimentary, ~300 Ma) and Deccan Traps (igneous, ~66 Ma) are separated by ~200 million years; they cannot form a continuous sequence; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct — option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a conflation trap — both Gondwana rocks and Deccan Traps are associated with the Indian subcontinent's ancient geological history and both are found in broadly overlapping regions of central India, making students assume they form part of the same sequence. In reality, Gondwana rocks are Permian sedimentary formations while Deccan Traps are Cretaceous volcanic rocks — separated by nearly 200 million years and entirely different in origin, composition, and resource character.
solution.final_explanation:
The Deccan Traps represent one of the most significant volcanic episodes in Earth's geological history.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 'Trap' is derived from the Swedish word for stairs — reflecting the stepped topography created by successive horizontal basalt flows. This is especially visible in Maharashtra's Sahyadri section of the Western Ghats.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Deccan Trap eruptions (~66 Ma) occurred near the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, releasing massive quantities of volcanic gases (SO₂, CO₂) that contributed to global climate disruption, potentially alongside the Chicxulub asteroid impact.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Gondwana rocks (Permian-Carboniferous, ~300–250 Ma) are sedimentary and coal-bearing; Deccan Traps are igneous basalt (~66 Ma). They are separated by ~200 million years and represent entirely different geological processes and periods.

Value Addition:
• The Deccan Traps cover approximately 500,000 km² — one of the world's largest volcanic provinces.
• Black cotton soil (Regur) from weathered Deccan Trap basalt is the primary agricultural soil of Maharashtra.
• India's major coalfields (Jharia, Raniganj, Singrauli) are all in Gondwana rock formations in Jharkhand, West Bengal, and MP.

solution.concept_anchor: Pachmarhi not in Eastern Ghats common confusion
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who confuse 'hills of central India' with Eastern Ghats may place Pachmarhi Hills within the Eastern Ghats system, especially since the question lists genuinely Eastern Ghats ranges in other options.
elimination_logic: Nallamala Hills — located in interior Andhra Pradesh; a documented Eastern Ghats range; belongs in the Eastern Ghats system.
Javadi Hills — located in Tamil Nadu (Tiruvannamalai/Vellore); part of the Eastern Ghats chain; belongs.
Shevaroy Hills — Salem district, Tamil Nadu; part of the Eastern Ghats system; belongs.

Pachmarhi Hills — located in Madhya Pradesh on the Satpura Range; it is part of the Satpura system, NOT the Eastern Ghats — Pachmarhi is the hill station of MP on the Satpuras. Option d is the correct answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Pachmarhi (Madhya Pradesh) is the most common confusion item for Eastern Ghats questions. The Eastern Ghats are a discontinuous series of hills across Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Tamil Nadu. Pachmarhi is located on the Satpura Range in MP — geographically and geologically a completely different hill system. Students who know Pachmarhi is a hill station with tribal significance may assume it belongs to the Eastern Ghats' tribal highland system.
solution.final_explanation:
The Eastern Ghats are a series of discontinuous, eroded hill ranges running in a NE-SW direction across eastern peninsular India.

• Option (a) — Belongs to Eastern Ghats: Nallamala Hills dominate interior Andhra Pradesh (Kurnool, Nellore, Prakasam districts) and are a well-documented part of the Eastern Ghats system.
• Option (b) — Belongs to Eastern Ghats: Javadi Hills (Tiruvannamalai-Vellore, Tamil Nadu) are part of the Eastern Ghats chain where it extends into Tamil Nadu.
• Option (c) — Belongs to Eastern Ghats: Shevaroy (Servarayan) Hills in Salem district, Tamil Nadu are part of the Eastern Ghats and host the Yercaud hill station.
• Option (d) — Does NOT belong: Pachmarhi Hills are part of the Satpura Range in Madhya Pradesh — a completely separate hill system between the Narmada and Tapti rivers. Pachmarhi is Madhya Pradesh's only hill station, located at the Satpura plateau.

Value Addition:
• The Eastern Ghats are composed of ancient Charnockite and Khondalite rocks — among India's oldest geological formations.
• The Satpura National Park and Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve are located in this Satpura system.
• Deomali (Odisha) and Jindhagada/Arma Konda (AP) are the two most cited candidates for the Eastern Ghats' highest peak.

solution.concept_anchor: Narmada estuary not delta westward rift valley flow

statement_analysis.statement: The Narmada River flows westward through a rift valley (graben) and forms an estuary near Bharuch where it meets the Gulf of Khambhat.
statement_analysis.reason: Narmada flows westward through the tectonic graben between Vindhyas and Satpuras, and terminates in a funnel-shaped estuary (not a delta) near Bharuch (Broach) in the Gulf of Khambhat — a well-established fact.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike most westward-flowing peninsular rivers, the Narmada has several major tributaries flowing in from the Vindhya side (northern bank) because of the steep Vindhyan escarpment.
statement_analysis.reason: The Narmada has LIMITED significant tributaries from the Vindhya (northern) side precisely because the steep Vindhyan escarpment creates abrupt valley walls that do not favour long tributary development; most tributaries come from the Satpura (southern) side.

statement_analysis.statement: The Tapti River, like the Narmada, flows westward through a tectonic graben and also terminates in an estuary rather than a delta.
statement_analysis.reason: The Tapti (Tapi) River flows westward through the Tapti graben (south of Satpuras) and forms an estuary at Surat — paralleling the Narmada's structural and hydrological character.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the Vindhyan escarpment is steep may wrongly accept Statement 2 as true, thinking 'steep = more runoff = more tributaries from north.'
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 — Narmada's westward flow through graben and estuary at Bharuch is standard; Statement 1 is CORRECT.

Evaluate Statement 2 — The steep Vindhyan escarpment actually LIMITS northern tributary development for the Narmada, not enhances it; major Narmada tributaries (Hiran, Burhner, Banjar) come from the Satpura south; Statement 2 is INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Tapti flowing westward through graben and forming an estuary at Surat mirrors the Narmada pattern; Statement 3 is CORRECT.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — option b (2 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 deploys a scope-extension trap by inverting the geographic logic. A steep escarpment on the north bank of the Narmada would logically seem to generate more runoff — and thus more tributaries — into the river. The reality is the opposite: the steep escarpment means very little catchment area, so the Vindhya side contributes few significant tributaries. This reverses intuition and traps students who reason from general geomorphic principles without recalling the specific case.
solution.final_explanation:
The Narmada and Tapti are India's two most significant westward-flowing peninsular rivers, both flowing through structural rift valleys.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Narmada occupies the Narmada graben (between Vindhyas and Satpuras), flows westward, and terminates in an estuary (not a delta) near Bharuch, Gulf of Khambhat. Estuaries, not deltas, form when rivers flow through narrow structural valleys without sufficient sediment spread.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Narmada's northern tributaries from the Vindhya escarpment are limited and insignificant. The Vindhyan escarpment is steep with minimal catchment; major tributaries (Hiran, Burhner, Banjar, Sher) come from the Satpura south bank.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Tapti (Tapi) occupies the Tapti graben south of the Satpuras, flows westward, and terminates in an estuary near Surat — a structural and hydrological parallel to the Narmada.

Value Addition:
• The Narmada is the longest west-flowing river in India and the largest river flowing into the Arabian Sea.
• Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada (in Gujarat) is one of India's most contested dam projects.
• Marble Rocks (Bhedaghat, MP) — famous gorge carved by Narmada through white marble — are located near Jabalpur.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may match Agasthyamalai with Kerala only (ignoring its Tamil Nadu extent) and incorrectly pair Anaimalai exclusively with Kerala, missing the district-level specificity.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Anamudi — it is unambiguously in the Anaimalai Hills (Idukki, Kerala); fixes A-3.
Doddabetta is the highest peak of the Nilgiris, located at Ooty (Nilgiris district, Tamil Nadu); fixes B-1.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap involves Anaimalai Hills and Nilgiris — both in the broader Kerala-Tamil Nadu Western Ghats zone. Students who know Doddabetta is the Nilgiris' highest but also know Anamudi is the Western Ghats' highest may confuse which peak belongs to which sub-range. Similarly, Agasthyamalai and Cardamom Hills are both in Kerala's south and may be swapped. Precise sub-range to feature mapping is the test here.
solution.final_explanation:
The southern Western Ghats are divided into distinct sub-ranges, each with characteristic peaks, ecosystems, and economic significance.

Correct matches:
• A (Anaimalai Hills) — 3 (Anamudi, 2,695 m): Anamudi, the highest peak in peninsular India, is located in the Anaimalai Hills in Idukki district, Kerala.
• B (Nilgiris) — 1 (Doddabetta, 2,637 m): Doddabetta is the highest peak of the Nilgiri Hills, located near Ooty (Udhagamandalam) in Tamil Nadu.
• C (Cardamom Hills) — 4 (Primary spice cultivation zone, Kerala): The Cardamom Hills (Elamalai) in Kerala's Idukki and Ernakulam districts are the country's primary cardamom-growing region.
• D (Agasthyamalai) — 2 (Proposed UNESCO WHS and endemic flora): Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve in the southernmost Western Ghats is known for extraordinary endemic plant diversity and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site candidate.

Trap pairing: Anaimalai and Nilgiris are frequently swapped because both contain famous high peaks.

Value Addition:
• The Agasthyamalai range is named after the sage Agastya, considered the cultural boundary between 'north' and 'south' India.
• Idukki district, Kerala contains both Anamudi and significant portions of the Cardamom Hills.
• Silent Valley (Nilambur, Kerala) — also in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve — is adjacent to the Anaimalai sub-range.
